title: ScreenShot: A Foundation Model for Few-Shot Combination Drug Screening
claim: A hierarchical architecture mirrors nested data structure, turning few-shot context observations into a prediction for a new query through staged encoders.
layout: 3 columns (data, model, output), left-to-right, red query path highlighted
description: A wide left-to-right diagram in three columns labeled Data, ScreenShot Foundation Model, and Output. On the left, a gray box of input drug combinations holds colored chips for drug, dose and viability, e.g. Drug A 10 µM, Drug B 1 µM, 80%. Below it, a red-outlined query box shows Drug E and Drug F with a dashed '?' for viability. The center is a dashed box with a vertical embedding bar. Inside, Level 1 stacks drug and dose embeddings into DCE blocks, followed by avg circles. Viability embeddings are added, and the results feed tall RE blocks at Level 2. Red arrows trace the query through DCE and RE, then into the SE block at Level 3. A LINEAR box follows, ending in a red 'PREDICTED 95%' box on the right. Blue, orange and purple mark drugs, green marks viability, and red marks the query path.
caption: Overview of the ScreenShot architecture. ScreenShot processes drug screening data through a three-level hierarchy. Level 1: all drug + dose embeddings are combined via self-attention within each drug combination by the Drug Combination Encoder (DCE). Level 2: query combinations attend to context observations (augmented with observed viability) via cross-attention through the Re- sponse Encoder (RE). Level 3: perturbation-level embeddings are aggregated via self-attention across the sample by the Sample Encoder (SE), producing a final representation for viability prediction.
abstract: Treating patients with combinations of drugs reduces the risk of resistance to any individual drug. Finding effective combinations is difficult because the large search space makes combinatorial screens prohibitively expensive, time consuming, and often technically infeasible. Predictive models can fill this gap, yet existing methods typically require molecular profiling of each sample and per-cohort training, limiting their applicability when time and tissue are scarce. To address this challenge, we introduce ScreenShot, a hierarchical transformer pretrained on 40 drug screening datasets covering 3,700 drugs and 6,000 biological samples, whose architecture mirrors the nested structure of screening data. Given a few-shot context of observations from a new patient, ScreenShot predicts the response of the sample to combination therapies through in-context learning, operating directly on functional measurements with no fine-tuning and no molecular profiling. On four held-out datasets, ScreenShot outperforms all baselines in both prediction accuracy and identification of selectively effective treatments. ScreenShot's internal representations are directly useful for experimental design: we use them to drive a weighted k-means++ active learning strategy that selects which experiments to run, achieving the same hit detection as uniform screening with a third of the budget. Source code and interactive dashboard: https://github.com/tansey-lab/screenshot.
